transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-11-23
Start time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Sam Carter (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Orion Ops CTO), Priya Nair (Orion Sr. ML Eng), Alex Gomez (Orion Infra)

Summary (auto): quick hosted API runthrough focused on chat/text generation. live demo of streaming, adjusting params, and handling retries. some questions on SLA/latency and security.

Transcript:
[00:00] Sam Carter: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — Sam from Redwood here, with Maya who is our solutions engineer. how's every— how's everyone doing?
[00:05] Jordan Lee: Good, thanks. excited to see the hosted api stuff.
[00:08] Priya Nair: Hi, yeah quick context — we're prototyping an assistant for ops runbooks, so latency is kinda important, and we have sensitive logs so data residency questions later.
[00:16] Maya Patel: Great context, thanks Priya. we'll focus on streaming and how params affect quality and latency. and we'll cover retries and idempotency so you can avoid double actions.
[00:23] Alex Gomez: Awesome. i'll be listening for networking and auth bits.
[00:26] Sam Carter: Quick agenda: 1) short product overview 2) demo: chat endpoint, streaming responses, parameters (temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop) 3) retry model and idempotency keys 4) Q&A and next steps.
[00:35] Jordan Lee: sounds good.
[01:05] Maya Patel: Ok jumping into demo — i'm sharing my screen, showing a simple cURL to the hosted /v1/chat/completions endpoint. so basic payload: model, messages array, and then stream=true to get partial tokens back. note — streaming uses server-sent events, you get data chunks as they generate.
[01:22] (screen share started)
[01:28] Maya Patel: Here's an example with stream: true. we show each delta chunk with role/content. you can render that progressively in the UI. streaming reduces perceived latency because you get first tokens sooner even if total compute is same.
[01:45] Priya Nair: when you say perceived latency — what's realistic for first-token time?
[01:52] Maya Patel: good q — depends on model and max_tokens and prompt length, but for a 2k context and a 100 token reply we often see first-token in 60-150ms on our recommended low-latency models in hosted regions. that's for our curated LLMs; custom larger models or longer contexts will be slower.
[02:12] Jordan Lee: 60-150 ms? that's in-range. what about tail latency and p95?
[02:17] Maya Patel: p95 is higher — often 200-400ms depending on traffic and batch window. if you need stricter SLOs we suggest dedicated or config adjustments like smaller batch windows and autoscaling rules.
[02:34] Alex Gomez: are there knobs for batching? we need predictable throughput.
[02:38] Maya Patel: yes — Redwood Optimize suggests batching sizes; runtime does continuous batching but you can set target latency and cost tradeoffs in the route config. for hosted you can pick low-latency profile which prioritizes smaller batches.
[02:51] Sam Carter: now on parameters — temperature controls randomness, top_p is nucleus sampling, max_tokens caps length and stop sequences let you terminate. small practical tip: for deterministic replies set temperature near 0 and use stop sequences — that helps for structured outputs.
[03:08] Priya Nair: do you recommend top_p instead of temperature?
[03:11] Maya Patel: they're complementary — top_p restricts to mass of probable tokens, temperature scales distribution. often teams tune temperature first.
[03:20] Jordan Lee: any examples of changing them affecting cost?
[03:23] Sam Carter: not directly cost per token, but higher temperature can lead to longer outputs if model meanders, so indirectly more tokens = higher cost.
[03:34] Maya Patel: demo time — i'll call the API with temperature 0.2 and max_tokens 120. watch streaming come in.
[03:48] (API call live; partial tokens appear)
[04:10] Maya Patel: you can see delta chunks: "data: {\"choices\":[{\"delta\":{\"content\":\"We recommend...\"}}]}" — the SDK pr abstracts this. in node/python SDK you can subscribe to on_delta events.
[04:28] Jordan Lee: are your SDKs open source?
[04:31] Sam Carter: yes node/python go clients are on GitHub; we'll send links.
[04:35] Priya Nair: retry behavior — if a request times out what's the right way to retry? we can't risk duplicates that trigger infra actions.
[04:44] Maya Patel: important. for idempotent operations (like triggers) we recommend two patterns: 1) use idempotency_key header for create-like actions; 2) for chat completions you can use a request_id/email and store server-side if the downstream side-effect is external. our hosted API supports idempotency_key for exactly-once semantics for up to 24 hours.
[05:05] Alex Gomez: and if streaming fails mid-way is there resume?
[05:09] Maya Patel: streaming can't resume mid-request — you'd need to re-request with same idempotency key and possibly a pointer to the last token; many customers do client-side dedupe or request a short summary. for long-running generation we recommend chunking or asynchronous jobs.
[05:26] Jordan Lee: ok ok. what about retries in SDKs — exponential backoff?
[05:30] Maya Patel: SDKs implement a default retry policy with jitter, exponential backoff, and classify errors (rate limit vs server error). but we recommend app-level logic for non-idempotent actions.
[05:42] Priya Nair: how configurable are rate limits per team?
[05:46] Sam Carter: hosted plans have tiered rate limits; for enterprise we can increase and add burst windows. Dedicated gives you reserved capacity which avoids noisy neighbor throttling.
[05:56] Jordan Lee: security quick hit — do you retain prompts and responses? we need to avoid storing PHI.
[06:02] Sam Carter: by default hosted logs are retained for 30 days for debugging, but we have options: short retention, no-logging mode, and Private deployment for air-gapped. enterprise contracts include custom retention. we'll share SOC2/ISO docs.
[06:16] Priya Nair: what's encryption at rest and KMS?
[06:19] Maya Patel: AES-256 at rest, and we integrate with customer KMS for dedicated/private. hosted managed uses our KMS but we can enable customer KMS for sensitive customers under enterprise agreement.
[06:31] Jordan Lee: good.
[06:35] Maya Patel: back to demo — i'll show a small retry scenario: triggering a 502 and SDK retry. you can see HTTP 502 classified as retryable with backoff. also show idempotency header usage.
[06:50] (demo showing header: Idempotency-Key: abc-123)
[07:02] Maya Patel: note: idempotency keys protect against duplicate side-effects but not duplicate token outputs if request partially succeeded. best practice: design side-effecting endpoints to be idempotent server-side.
[07:18] Jordan Lee: for our use case we will call external infra automation — so we need guaranteed once. sounds like private/dedicated might be safer?
[07:26] Sam Carter: yes dedicated with reserved capacity plus idempotency patterns is the high-assurance route. hosted can work but requires app-level safeguards.
[07:35] Priya Nair: costs? high level comparison?
[07:38] Sam Carter: hosted is pay-as-you-go per token with tiered pricing; dedicated is committed monthly with much lower per-token unit economics but a baseline commit. i'll send a one-pager.
[07:51] Alex Gomez: curious about regional latency — do you have EU/US regions?
[07:55] Maya Patel: hosted has multiple regions (US, EU, APAC upcoming). you can pin a route to a region to satisfy data residency.
[08:05] Jordan Lee: what's typical onboarding time for a POC? we aim to ship an MVP in 3 weeks.
[08:10] Sam Carter: very doable — we have quickstart templates and a 2-4 week POC pack for infra integration and basic evals.
[08:18] Maya Patel: we'll include a benchmark spreadsheet — give us a prompt set and we'll run latency/cost numbers across our recommended models.
[08:25] Priya Nair: can the benchmark include streaming first-token times and p95?
[08:28] Maya Patel: yes we'll capture first-token, p50, p95, and token cost.
[08:33] Jordan Lee: any known gotchas with stop sequences when streaming? sometimes clients see truncated final tokens.
[08:40] Maya Patel: stop sequences are applied at generation time; sometimes a partial chunk includes the stop and then extra buffering causes small duplication. SDKs provide cleaning utilities. recommended practice: detect stop on the client and truncate accordingly.
[08:55] Sam Carter: quick note on observability — console shows per-route latency, token breakdown, cost by token type, and tracing hooks. helps debug where cost is coming from.
[09:05] Alex Gomez: do you have per-user quotas? we need per-tenant isolation.
[09:09] Sam Carter: yes RBAC and quotas per-team; enterprise customers can map routes to projects and limit by API key.
[09:16] Priya Nair: ok great.
[09:20] Jordan Lee: can you send a sample contract/SLAs for latency?
[09:24] Sam Carter: sure — standard hosted SLA is 99.9 for api availability; dedicated offers stronger latency and availability options. legal & pricing will follow up.
[09:34] Maya Patel: any final technical Qs before we wrap?
[09:38] Priya Nair: one more — is there a recommended pattern for streaming long multi-turn conversations and state?
[09:43] Maya Patel: yes store conversation history server-side, send condensed context (summaries) to keep prompt sizes manageable. we also support KV cache for private deployments; for hosted you can use the conversation_id pattern in the SDK for convenience.
[09:58] Jordan Lee: good.
[10:02] Sam Carter: ok recap: we'll send pricing and hosted vs dedicated comparison, share SDK links and benchmark spreadsheet, and schedule a POC call with Alex and infra next week. action items in the notes.
[10:15] Jordan Lee: thanks everyone. we'll share prompt sets by Monday.
[10:18] Sam Carter: perfect — thanks, talk soon.
[10:22] (call ended)

Notes on transcription: occasional misheard words (e.g., "idempo" for idempotency) and punctuation may be imperfect; speaker labels are best-effort.
